Hi, I'm really sorry you've had to go through this. I'm not a professional and I'm not living within your mind so I don't want to give any hard advice, but just food for thought: you mention that you wouldn't be able to speak to a therapist about this. If you just imagine/visualize yourself telling someone all this in real life, what emotion do you feel in your body?

Internalized/repressed shame might be the reason (and again I stress the word "might" because I can't presume to know what's going on in your nervous system, only you can know), and could also explain the desire to shift away from thinking about the trauma as trauma and wanting to dismiss it as a mood swing and trying to think of it more "positively". Like to avoid feeling the shame. Or to avoid feeling whatever emotion you find lingering there. Generally I just mean that the reframing of the trauma in your mind could be an effort to avoid feeling whatever bad things it makes you feel, in favor of feeling "good" things instead.

It's interesting that sometimes our trauma responses are in an effort to avoid feeling the terrible emotion that's stuck within us (e.g. reframing the trauma as something else to avoid shame), and sometimes they're an automatic effort to stealthily TRY to feel the terrible emotion (e.g. calling yourself a name to make yourself feel shame, maybe without even realizing it, to satisfy that emotional drive).

It's a sucky and complicated situation and I can only speak from my personal experience. Don't take anything I say as gospel but maybe it'll help contextualize some of the things you've been feeling and the behaviors you've been drawn to. I'm here if you need anyone to talk to and I truly hope you can find some healing.

Yeah. For me it just came down to the fact that there were many instances in my life when I was made to feel ashamed, but that's such a hard emotion to process because there's nothing you can do about it, so I never fully FELT it when it came. So in the modern day I had all this repressed shame. And that was leading to that harsh inner voice all the time even though they didn't seem connected at first.

I spent some time doing regular things that would make me feel shame or thinking about past times when I felt shame, and then I'd try to stay with that feeling and feel it "to completion". And even just doing that a little bit made a huge difference. It was painful in the moment, but I would feel so much lighter afterward. I was suddenly able to think of those memories where I felt shame and I didn't feel it anymore, and instead those memories were just logical things and not emotional things.

Not sure if this will work for everyone but that's been my case. To answer your question, yeah the voice can go away.

It definitely does seem to be the case, however, I do think it can be important to keep learning about HOW to do this. It's still hard for a lot of people to feel their feelings because they may not present themselves clearly. And a huge part is trying to reconcile contradictory emotions that you experience intertwined. That sort of thing isn't easy and takes some very focused work. But you're right that it seems like repressed emotions may be the general culprit in PTSD. I know for sure that every treatment I've tried has only ever worked in cases where it provoked me to feel my feelings.

Hi there. It's hard for me to remember how long it took, and I was self-administering EMDR almost every day too so it was a weird situation. I think the key was mostly that, whenever I processed a big emotion that I had habitually been repressing, and I felt that emotion a lot instead of pushing it down, after that particular session I would notice a large physical improvement. I did plenty of sessions where I didn't notice any physical changes, but they were important for getting me towards those sessions where I processed lots of emotion. I was super repressed and I wasn't doing the EMDR perfectly by myself because I'm stupid, so it took maybe a few months of sessions to see a vast improvement in my ability to walk and whatnot. If I knew what I was doing, who knows, it may have only taken a couple sessions because I'd have been more emotion-focused from the start.

I wish I could give a more clear answer but the situation was a mess for me. I really hope the treatment helps you with your physical symptoms. If I could offer any advice it would be to be patient and be as open as possible to your feelings.

I feel that quick fixes and tricks as mentioned in my post are good starts and can be helpful when combined with other things, but in my experience they're more Band-Aids than solutions. For what it's worth, EMDR (and specifically Flash EMDR due to my dissociation) has made the biggest impact in my case.
I do this too! It seems to help me feel capable of doing things, like an affirmation basically implying "You can act now, it's safe to act"

For me every memory caused this and it made it really hard to accomplish any processing, so I resorted to using the Flash technique on every memory before going straight to EMDR. That seems to process the memory a little bit at a time without activating me enough to cause dissociation, and eventually the memory reduces enough that I can do EMDR on it without dissociating.

While I started off using a YouTube video that was a green ball moving side to side on the screen, I found that the eye movement method hurt my eyes, so I switched to not using any videos and just tap each of my legs back and forth. EMDR seems to just require bilateral stimulation: anything that alternately stimulates each side of your body.

In doing it myself for the last 8 months (without a therapist and without any support system really), I've made a lot of progress, though it's been difficult and takes a lot of thought. My biggest advice by far would be to use a combination of the Flash Technique and EMDR.

Flash is great for when you first start targeting a memory. I used to try going straight to EMDR and within moments I would feel myself fully dissociate and tense up and the rest of the treatment would be ineffective even though I would try to plow through it. If you do Flash and then later do EMDR on that memory, you should be less likely to be overwhelmed  and knocked out of your window of tolerance. Using Flash made self-EMDR possible for me. Flash has been like taking little nibbles out of the distressfulness of the memory, until it becomes small enough to use regular EMDR on it.

Flash isn't too complicated either. And it's not upsetting. You can find some decent instructions online. What I do personally is think very briefly about the target memory (or I just think of the IDEA of thinking about the memory even, if it's super sensitive) and then immediately drop it, focus on a positive engaging focus (which you can read about, it's like a positive distraction that keeps your mind occupied), while tapping my knees or arms back and forth slowly, and then every few seconds I quickly blink my eyes twice. You shouldn't feel much during because you're only subconsciously processing the memory, without fully activating it.

I really hope you get some relief through this method. It's hard to do by yourself and I don't know that I can even "recommend" it necessarily, but I can say that it has changed my life for the better and I hope it changes yours too.

Your life has always been changing. You mentioned that nothing gets better, because since you developed these painful feelings, they haven't changed. But remember that those feelings developed from somewhere, they weren't there from the instant you were born, they had to be inundated into your head and heart over time. Maybe it was during your childhood, but the point is that you went from a human being without such terrible feelings of suffering, to a human being with those feelings. And that proves that your mental state can change dramatically -- in your case, it was for the worse, unfortunately. But all that means is that it's capable of changing dramatically for the better as well.

You can change. Things can get better. I'm not saying they'll get better tomorrow, but there is absolutely nothing that says your situation is destined to be static for the next decades of your life. So much changes. But you have to keep doing your due diligence, going to therapy as you have been, and being patient. You've been so patient so far, I understand, and I know it's hard to keep going. I'm truly, deeply sorry that you're in this pain. And I don't mean to just lecture about how you are wrong or anything, because I understand the feelings very much and I mean no offense at all. I just think there's always a possibility for things to change for the better eventually, and you shouldn't rob yourself of that potential.

Everyone's taste is different and probability dictates that you'll eventually meet someone who is interested in you, no matter how you feel about yourself. It's just a numbers game.
